title: High-Pressure/High-Dose Versus Standard PIPAC in Epithelioid Peritoneal Mesothelioma: Safety, Feasibility, and Outcomes From a Bicentric Comparative Cohort Study.
authors: Kockelmann F, Michot N, Demtröder CRD et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pressurized intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy (PIPAC) is a minimally invasive option for peritoneal mesothelioma (PeM) in patients not eligible for cytoreductive surgery (CRS) and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC). This bicentric study compared the safety, feasibility, and sex-specific outcomes of standard versus high-pressure/high-dose PIPAC (HP/HD-PIPAC).
METHODS: Patients who had non-resectable epithelioid PeM (ePeM) treated with PIPAC at two German centers were retrospectively analyzed. Group 1 received standard PIPAC (cisplatin 7.5 mg/m2 + doxorubicin 1.5 mg/m2, 12 mmHg), and group 2 received HP/HD-PIPAC (cisplatin 20 mg/m2 + doxorubicin 4 mg/m2, 20 mmHg). Procedural outcomes, postoperative complications, interval from diagnosis to first PIPAC, and overall survival (OS) were analyzed. Uni- and multivariable Cox regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with OS.
RESULTS: The 46 patients in the study (group 1: 25 patients; group 2: 21 patients) underwent 120 of 132 scheduled PIPAC procedures. The median OS from diagnosis was 48 months overall: 48 months in group 1, and 36 months in group 2. The interval from diagnosis to first PIPAC was shorter in group 2 (2 vs. 20 months; p = 0.009). Severe complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥III) occurred in 6.2 % of group 1 versus 2.9 % of group 2. The median OS was 106 months for the females versus 35 months for the males (p = 0.064). Multivariable analysis identified female sex, bidirectional treatment, and a longer interval between diagnosis and first PIPAC as independent factors associated with improved OS.
CONCLUSIONS: The HP/HD-PIPAC regimen is feasible and safe. Although no significant survival differences were observed between treatment groups, prospective studies are required to define the optimal timing and integration of PIPAC within multimodal treatment strategies. Findings should be interpreted in the context of the retrospective study design.

title: Surgical Approaches and Extent of Resection for Non-myasthenic Thymic Epithelial Tumors:Current Evidence and Future Perspectives.
authors: Takizawa H, Endo H, Abe Y et al.
abstract: Thymic epithelial tumors are rare anterior mediastinal neoplasms that include thymoma, thymic carcinoma, and neuroendocrine tumors. Complete surgical resection remains the cornerstone of curative treatment;however, the optimal extent of thymectomy and surgical approach are still being debated. Advances in minimally invasive techniques, such as video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and robot-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (RATS), have shifted practice away from traditional median sternotomy. Evidence consistently shows that complete resection is the most important prognostic factor across all subtypes. Regarding early-stage thymoma, multicenter and propensity score-matched studies showed that partial thymectomy may achieve similar oncologic outcomes to total thymectomy, with shorter hospital stays and reduced perioperative morbidity. Conversely, total thymectomy remains essential for thymic carcinoma or invasive disease. Minimally invasive approaches, particularly RATS, offer advantages including precise dissection in narrow mediastinal spaces, less blood loss, and faster recovery without compromising the margin status or long-term survival. Emerging data also suggest potential long-term immunological and oncologic consequences of total thymectomy in adults, underscoring the need for individualized surgical planning. Overall, current evidence supports tailoring the extent and approach of thymectomy according to the histological subtype, tumor stage, and patient factors, balancing oncologic radicality with the preservation of physiological thymic function. title: CD19 CAR T cell therapy reshapes the host microbiota immune axis in autoimmune diseases
summary: CD19 targeted CAR T cell therapy induces profound B cell depletion and clinical responses in autoimmune disease; however, whether it reshapes host microbiota interactions remains unknown. We longitudinally profiled gut microbiome composition and microbiota-specific humoral immunity in 20 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, or idiopathic inflammatory myopathy undergoing CAR T cell therapy, alongside 23 healthy controls, using shotgun metagenomics, IgA/IgG-bound microbiota profiling, and PhIP Seq. CAR T cell therapy reshaped microbiota directed humoral immunity, with reduced fecal IgA and serum anti commensal IgA and IgG accompanied by selective remodeling of microbiota-reactive antibody repertoires. This finding was paralleled by selective changes in gut microbial composition, including depletion of Bifidobacterium adolescentis, without uniform depletion of disease-associated pathobionts. Integrated host microbiome analyses identified altered predicted protein protein interactions involving the immunoproteasome and B cell plasma cell pathways, with interactions before CAR T cell intervention being significantly associated with subsequent relapse. Consistent with these findings, taxon specific IgA targeting, but not global diversity of IgA IgG coated microbiota, differed according to subsequent relapse. Lower baseline fecal IgA was also associated with delayed B-cell reconstitution, linking mucosal humoral immunity to immune recovery after CAR T cell therapy.
